title: 〜くらい・〜ぐらい (downplaying / bare minimum)
meaning: Presents something as “just a small thing,” showing that it is not worth much; or marks the bare minimum: “at least this much (should be done).”
connection: Noun / verb plain form + くらい・ぐらい

senses.label: Downplaying: just ...
senses.meaning: The speaker sees the matter as minor and not worth mentioning, like “just” or “a mere.” It often takes 「で」 as 「〜くらいで」: “just because of something so small.” It usually carries criticism or annoyance.
senses.connection: Noun / verb ta-form + くらいで・ぐらいで (often with 「そんな」「ちょっと」「一度」)
examples: Don't give up just because you failed once.
I can't take a day off work for a mere cold.
Do something that simple yourself.

senses.label: Bare minimum
senses.meaning: Means “at least do this much.” The speaker sees it as the most basic expectation, often with a sense of “you can't even do that?” It often pairs with 「せめて」.
senses.connection: Noun + くらい（は）・ぐらい（は） + verb (なさい／てほしい／てくれてもいい, etc.)
examples: At least say hello.
If you're going to be late, you could at least call.
Please at least write your name.

notes: 「くらい」 and 「ぐらい」 mean the same thing. 「ぐらい」 is more common in speech.
After a number or quantity, it means “about” (「10分くらい」). That is a different use, with no downplaying.
「〜くらいなら」 means “rather than ..., I'd sooner ...” and is a separate grammar point.

daily.title: A parent scolding a child
daily.description: The child won't even do simple things, and the parent complains.
daily.example: At least clean your own room yourself.

daily.title: Comforting a heartbroken friend
daily.description: Telling a friend not to get down over one setback.
daily.example: Don't get so down just because you got dumped once.

daily.title: Complaining about a family member
daily.description: Showing annoyance at someone who came home late.
daily.example: If you're going to be late, at least send a message.

work.title: A senior reminding a new hire
work.description: A senior colleague points out the most basic manners.
work.example: When you're going to be late, please at least let us know.

work.title: A boss encouraging a team member
work.description: The boss tells them not to lose heart over a small mistake.
work.example: No need to be down over a mistake this small.

etymology: 「くらい」 comes from the noun 「位（くらい）」, “rank” or “position.” From “rank” it came to mean “degree,” and then “a low degree, nothing more,” which gives the downplaying sense. 「ぐらい」 is the voiced variant.

similar.title: 〜くらい・〜ぐらい (degree)
similar.explanation: The degree use means “to the point of ...” (「泣きたいくらい痛い」) and describes a degree objectively. This use stresses that the degree is low and not worth mentioning, with a subjective judgment.

similar.title: 〜なんか・〜など (downplaying)
similar.explanation: 「なんか」 belittles the thing itself (「勉強なんか嫌いだ」). 「くらい」 stresses that the matter is small: “even something this small ...”.

similar.title: 〜さえ
similar.explanation: 「さえ」 means “even,” giving an extreme example. 「くらい」 means “at least this much,” a minimum demand. 「挨拶さえしない」 is an exclamation; 「挨拶ぐらいしなさい」 is a demand.

title: 〜というか (or rather)
meaning: Corrects or adds to what was just said: “or rather,” “I'd say it's more like ...”. In speech, it also starts a sentence to switch topics.
connection: Noun / adjective / verb plain form + というか (casual: っていうか)

senses.label: Rephrasing
senses.meaning: The speaker feels the first word isn't quite right and offers a better one: “or rather,” “more precisely.” It is softer than 「というより」 and often sounds hesitant.
senses.connection: Noun / adjective / verb plain form + というか、〜
examples: He's more like a friend than a teacher.
This dish isn't so much spicy as kind of painful.

senses.label: How should I put it
senses.meaning: 「何というか」「なんていうか」 shows you can't find the right words: “how should I put it.” Used to describe feelings vaguely or gently.
senses.connection: 何（なん） + というか・ていうか
examples: How should I put it... he's a mysterious person.
How do I say this... it's a feeling I can't put into words.

senses.label: Sentence-initial: by the way / actually
senses.meaning: Young people put it at the start of a sentence to change the topic: “anyway,” “actually.” It can also brush aside what the other person said. Very casual; not used in formal settings.
senses.connection: Sentence start: っていうか、〜／というか、〜
examples: Actually, shall we just go home?
Wait, who did you hear that from?

notes: 「っていうか」 and 「てゆうか」 are spoken forms and are not used in writing.
「〜というか〜というか」 lists two descriptions (“you could call it ... or ...”) and is a separate grammar point.
「〜というから」 means “because (someone) said ...” and is not this grammar point.

daily.title: Describing someone to a friend
daily.description: Not sure how to describe your impression, so you think out loud.
daily.example: She's not so much beautiful as cute.

daily.title: Young people chatting
daily.description: A sudden change of topic between friends.
daily.example: Anyway, what are we doing about tomorrow's test?

daily.title: Putting mixed feelings into words
daily.description: Sharing your thoughts after a movie.
daily.example: How should I put it... it was a really thought-provoking movie.

work.title: Rewording in a meeting
work.description: A speaker corrects the word they just used.
work.example: It's not a problem exactly, but there's something I'm a bit concerned about.

etymology: Made of the quoting particle 「と」 + 「いう（言う）」 + the question particle 「か」 expressing uncertainty. Literally “should I call it ...?”, which led to the correcting sense “or rather.” In speech 「と」 becomes 「って」, giving 「っていうか」.

similar.title: 〜というより
similar.explanation: 「というより」 clearly rejects the first item and favors the second, and is more formal. 「というか」 is softer and more hesitant, mostly spoken.

similar.title: 〜というか〜というか
similar.explanation: Lists two descriptions without settling on one (「無謀というか大胆というか」). A single 「というか」 just corrects what came before.

similar.title: つまり
similar.explanation: 「つまり」 restates or sums up what was said. 「というか」 corrects something that felt inaccurate.

title: 〜てくれと言う・〜なと言う (reported requests and orders)
meaning: Reports someone else's request, prohibition, or order: “(someone) told me to ... / told me not to ...”.
connection: Verb te-form + くれと言う; verb dictionary form + なと言う; verb imperative form + と言う

senses.label: Reporting a request
senses.meaning: Reports a 「〜てくれ」 request: “(someone) asked me to ...”. Common as 「〜てくれと言われた」 and 「〜てくれと頼まれた」. A negative request is 「〜ないでくれと言う」.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + くれと言う／頼む; verb nai-form + ないでくれと言う
examples: A friend asked me to help him move.
My mom told me to come home earlier.
He told me not to tell anyone.

senses.label: Reporting a prohibition
senses.meaning: Reports a 「〜な」 prohibition: “(someone) told me not to ...”. Direct and strong; usually words from a boss, parent, or teacher.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + なと言う／なって言う
examples: The doctor told me not to drink.
My dad told me not to stay out late.

senses.label: Reporting an order
senses.meaning: Reports words in the imperative form: “(someone) ordered me to ...”. Very strong; used to pass on a strict order.
senses.connection: Verb imperative form (しろ／来い／寝ろ, etc.) + と言う・って言う
examples: My teacher told me to study harder.
The department manager told me to come right away.

notes: When reporting, keep the original request or command form and add 「と言う」. The person addressed is usually left out.
Compared with 「〜ように言う」, this is closer to the original words and sounds more direct.
In speech, people often say 「〜てくれって言われた」 and 「〜なって言われた」.

daily.title: Complaining about your parents to a friend
daily.description: Reporting what your parents demanded.
daily.example: My parents told me to quit my part-time job.

daily.title: Passing on a message
daily.description: Relaying a friend's request.
daily.example: Tanaka said he wants you to pick him up at the station.

daily.title: Explaining why you don't drink
daily.description: Telling why you're skipping alcohol.
daily.example: My doctor's told me not to drink.

work.title: Passing on a boss's words to a coworker
work.description: Relaying the boss's instructions.
work.example: The section chief said he wants you to fix these documents by today.

work.title: Explaining a confidentiality request
work.description: Passing on what the client asked you not to do.
work.example: The client has told us not to let this leak outside.

etymology: Built from direct speech + the quoting particle 「と」 + 「言う」. 「〜てくれ」 is the imperative of the giving verb 「くれる」, and 「な」 is a sentence-ending particle of prohibition. Embedding the original words in the sentence makes it a report.

similar.title: 〜ように言う (indirect order)
similar.explanation: 「〜ように言う」 is an indirect report and sounds softer. 「〜てくれと言う」 and 「〜なと言う」 keep the original words, so they sound more direct and vivid.

similar.title: 〜な (prohibition)
similar.explanation: 「〜な」 states a prohibition directly. 「〜なと言う」 reports someone else's prohibition.

similar.title: 〜と言う (quotation)
similar.explanation: 「と言う」 is general quotation. This grammar point specifically quotes requests, prohibitions, and orders.

meaning: The honorific form of 「である」. It raises the person being talked about when describing their identity or state.
connection: Noun / na-adjective stem + でいらっしゃる

senses.label: Honorific “to be”
senses.meaning: Same as 「〜です／〜である」, but shows respect. Describes the other person's identity, job, or attributes. The subject must be someone you respect.
senses.connection: Noun + でいらっしゃいます（か）
examples: This is Professor Yamada.
Excuse me, but are you Mr. Tanaka?

senses.label: Respectful description of a state
senses.meaning: Follows a na-adjective to describe someone's state or personality respectfully. Common in greetings and compliments.
senses.connection: Na-adjective stem + でいらっしゃる (お元気でいらっしゃいますか, etc.)
examples: How have you been?
The company president is a very gentle person.
Our teacher has been passionate ever since she was young.

notes: Never use it for yourself or your own side: ✕「私は田中でいらっしゃいます」. Say 「田中でございます」 instead.
「ていらっしゃる」 (読んでいらっしゃる) is the honorific of 「ている」. Don't confuse the two.
It conjugates like 「いらっしゃる」; the masu-form is 「いらっしゃいます」.

daily.title: Calling an older relative
daily.description: Checking in on someone you haven't talked to in a while.
daily.example: Grandma, I hope you've been well as always.

daily.title: Talking about a friend's parent
daily.description: Complimenting a friend's father.
daily.example: So your father is a doctor.

work.title: Receiving a client
work.description: The receptionist confirms a visitor's identity.
work.example: Excuse me, but are you Mr. Suzuki from ABC Trading?

work.title: Introducing a superior
work.description: Introducing a company executive to a client.
work.example: This is Sato, our senior managing director.

work.title: Greeting in a business letter
work.description: Opening line of an email.
work.example: I trust this finds you all in good health.

etymology: Made of 「で」 (the conjunctive form of the copula 「だ」) + 「いらっしゃる」, the honorific of 「いる／来る／行く」. In other words, the 「ある」 of 「である」 is swapped for an honorific verb.

similar.title: 〜でございます
similar.explanation: 「でございます」 is polite language and can be used for your own side (「田中でございます」). 「でいらっしゃる」 is honorific and only for others.

similar.title: 〜である
similar.explanation: 「である」 is a neutral, written “to be.” 「でいらっしゃる」 is a respectful way to describe a person.

similar.title: いらっしゃる・おっしゃる
similar.explanation: On its own, 「いらっしゃる」 means “to be, come, go.” With 「で」 in front, it means “to be (someone/something).”

meaning: Works with a negative to mean “not at all,” stressing a complete negation.
connection: まったく（全く） + verb nai-form / negative adjective / noun + がない

senses.label: Not at all
senses.meaning: Stresses that an action or state does not happen at all: “not at all,” “absolutely not.” Stronger than 「あまり〜ない」. Slightly more formal than 「ぜんぜん」; fine in both speech and writing.
senses.connection: まったく + verb nai-form／ません (全く知らない／全く分からない, etc.)
examples: I had no idea about that at all.
I can't understand a thing he's saying.
I couldn't sleep at all last night.

senses.label: None whatsoever
senses.meaning: Pairs with 「〜がない」 or 「〜ではない」 to say something is completely absent: “no ... whatsoever.” Often used with nouns like 「関係」「問題」「興味」.
senses.connection: まったく + noun がない／noun ではない／adjective くない
examples: This matter has nothing whatsoever to do with me.
That movie wasn't interesting at all.

notes: 「まったく」 can also be used in positive sentences to mean “completely” or “truly” (「全く同じだ」「全くその通りだ」).
On its own, 「まったく！」 or 「まったくもう」 expresses annoyance, like “Honestly!” or “Good grief.”
The kanji is 「全く」, read 「まったく」. Don't read it as 「ぜんく」.

daily.title: A friend brings up gossip
daily.description: Saying you had no idea.
daily.example: What, those two are dating? I didn't notice at all.

daily.title: Complaining after a test
daily.description: Telling a classmate the test was too hard.
daily.example: I couldn't solve the last question at all.

daily.title: Watching a foreign movie
daily.description: Telling a friend you can't follow it.
daily.example: Without subtitles, I don't understand a thing.

work.title: Responding to a client's concern
work.description: Assuring the client there will be no impact.
work.example: This change will have no impact whatsoever.

work.title: News report
work.description: Describing a situation in the news.
work.example: The cause of the accident is still completely unknown.

etymology: 「まったく」 is written 「全く」 and comes from the conjunctive form of the classical adjective 「全し（まったし）」, meaning “whole, complete.” With a negative, it stresses “not at all.”

similar.title: ぜんぜん〜ない
similar.explanation: Similar meaning. 「ぜんぜん」 is more casual; 「まったく」 is a bit more formal, and news and written texts prefer 「全く」.

similar.title: ちっとも〜ない
similar.explanation: 「ちっとも」 is only spoken and often sounds irritated. 「まったく」 has a wider range of use.

similar.title: 決して〜ない
similar.explanation: 「決して」 expresses strong will or assertion (“never”). 「まったく」 only describes the degree: “not at all.”

title: 〜つまり (sentence-initial: in other words)
meaning: Restates what came before in other words, or draws a conclusion: “in other words,” “so,” “basically.”
connection: Sentence start / mid-sentence: A。つまり、B／A、つまりB

senses.label: In other words
senses.meaning: Restates the preceding content more simply or directly: “that is,” “namely.” A and B refer to the same thing.
senses.connection: Noun A、つまり noun B (A and B are the same thing)
examples: He's my mother's older brother, in other words my uncle.
There's a meeting next Friday, that is, on the 10th.

senses.label: Drawing a conclusion
senses.meaning: Sums up what was said into a conclusion or the real point: “so,” “basically.” Often pairs with 「〜ということだ」 or 「〜わけだ」 at the end.
senses.connection: Sentence start: つまり、〜ということだ／〜わけだ
examples: So you're saying you don't want to go, right?
The trains have stopped. So I can't get home today.

senses.label: Asking for the point
senses.meaning: Used alone as 「つまり？」 or 「つまり何が言いたいの」 to push the other person to get to the point. Common in speech; can sound impatient.
senses.connection: つまり？／つまり何〜
examples: So what are you trying to say?

notes: 「つまり」 works in both speech and writing. A more formal word is 「すなわち」, and a more casual one is 「要するに」.
「とどのつまり」 is an idiom meaning “in the end,” “when all is said and done.”
It can be written 「詰まり」 in kanji, but as a conjunction it is usually written in kana.

daily.title: A friend is beating around the bush
daily.description: Your friend talks for ages, so you sum it up.
daily.example: So you want me to lend you money?

daily.title: Explaining a family relationship
daily.description: Explaining to a friend how you're related.
daily.example: That's my dad's younger sister, in other words my aunt.

work.title: Wrapping up a meeting
work.description: The chair sums up the discussion.
work.example: So this term's goal is a ten percent increase in sales, correct?

work.title: Explaining data
work.description: Telling your boss what the numbers mean.
work.example: Users have dropped by half. In other words, we need to take action.

etymology: From 「詰まり」, the conjunctive form of the verb 「詰まる（つまる）」, “to be packed, to reach the end.” “Reaching the end” led to “ultimately, in short,” and it came to be used as a conjunction.

similar.title: 要するに
similar.explanation: 「要するに」 is more casual and focuses on “to put it simply.” 「つまり」 can both rephrase and conclude, so it is more versatile.

similar.title: すなわち
similar.explanation: 「すなわち」 is formal, written language, mostly for exact restatement. 「つまり」 works in both speech and writing.

similar.title: 〜ということだ (hearsay / conclusion)
similar.explanation: Often pairs with 「つまり」 as 「つまり〜ということだ」, stating the conclusion at the end of the sentence.

title: 〜そのため (sentence-initial: therefore / to that end)
meaning: Refers back to what was just said to mean “therefore” (cause) or “for that purpose” (goal). Mostly used in explanatory writing and formal settings.

senses.label: Therefore (cause)
senses.meaning: The first sentence is the cause, the second the result: “therefore,” “for this reason.” States cause and effect objectively; common in news, reports, and explanations. The second sentence cannot be a command or request.
senses.connection: A (cause)。そのため、B (result)
examples: It snowed heavily last night. As a result, the trains are stopped.
A typhoon is approaching. For this reason, the game has been canceled.

senses.label: For that purpose (goal)
senses.meaning: The first sentence is a goal, and the second is what is done to reach it: “to that end,” “for that.” Often 「そのために」.
senses.connection: A (goal)。そのために、B (action)
examples: I want to study abroad next year. To that end, I study English every day.
I'm planning to buy a new house. That's why I'm saving money.

notes: It is 「その」 + the formal noun 「ため」. 「そのため」 can also be written 「その為」.
For cause, the second sentence is usually an objective fact that has already happened, not a wish or command. For subjective judgments, use 「だから」.
「そのための〜」 modifies a noun, as in 「そのための準備」 (preparation for that).

daily.title: Explaining why you're late
daily.description: Telling a friend why you're late.
daily.example: There was an accident. Because of that, the bus was late.

daily.title: Talking about your goal
daily.description: Telling a friend what you're working toward.
daily.example: I want to run a marathon. That's why I go running every morning.

work.title: News report
work.description: The news explains traffic conditions.
work.example: Heavy rain has caused the river to rise. As a result, some roads are closed.

work.title: Notice to customers
work.description: A notice explaining a service interruption.
work.example: We will be carrying out system maintenance. For this reason, the service will be temporarily suspended tomorrow.

work.title: Business proposal
work.description: Stating a goal and the measures for it.
work.example: We aim to enter overseas markets. To that end, we will hire local staff.

etymology: Made of the demonstrative 「その」 + the formal noun 「ため（為）」. Since 「ため」 itself marks both cause and purpose, 「そのため」 also has both meanings: “therefore” and “for that purpose.”

similar.title: 〜ために
similar.explanation: 「〜ために」 attaches directly inside a sentence (「雨のために」). 「そのため」 starts a sentence, with 「その」 pointing back to what came before.

similar.title: それで
similar.explanation: 「それで」 is more casual and often used when narrating events. 「そのため」 is more formal, common in reports and news.

similar.title: だから
similar.explanation: 「だから」 is subjective and can be followed by commands or intentions. 「そのため」 shows objective cause and effect; the second part is usually a fact.

title: 〜ところで (sentence-initial: by the way)
meaning: Starts a sentence to close the current topic and move on to a new one: “by the way,” “oh, and,” “incidentally.”

senses.label: Changing the topic
senses.meaning: Moves the conversation from what was being discussed to something unrelated: “by the way.” The two topics are usually unconnected.
senses.connection: Sentence start: ところで、 + new topic
examples: It's hot today, isn't it? By the way, how's work going?
By the way, what happened with that matter?

senses.label: Asking in passing
senses.meaning: Brings up something you want to know during a conversation: “by the way, may I ask ...”. Usually leads into a question; sounds natural and polite.
senses.connection: ところで、〜ですか／〜の？
examples: By the way, how's Tanaka doing?
Oh, by the way, what time does tomorrow's meeting start again?

notes: 「Verb ta-form + ところで」 means “even if ... (it's no use)” and is a separate grammar point.
「さて」 also changes topics, but it is mostly used to get to the main point. 「ところで」 usually moves to a side topic.
Switching topics abruptly with 「ところで」 can sound unnatural. In business, finish one topic before using it.

daily.title: Chatting with a friend
daily.description: After talking about the weather, asking how things are.
daily.example: By the way, how are things with your girlfriend lately?

daily.title: Changing the subject at dinner
daily.description: Bringing up weekend plans at a family meal.
daily.example: Oh, by the way, want to go somewhere this weekend?

work.title: Shifting topics in a business meeting
work.description: After the main business, asking about something else.
work.example: By the way, did you have a chance to look at the documents I sent the other day?

work.title: Adding a point in an email
work.description: Raising another matter in the second half of an email.
work.example: On another note, regarding next month's trade show, would that time work for you?

etymology: Made of the formal noun 「ところ（所）」 + the particle 「で」, originally “at this place (moment).” Used at the start of a sentence, it came to mean “at this point (moving to another topic),” and became a topic-changing conjunction.

similar.title: 〜たところで
similar.explanation: After a verb ta-form, it means “even if ..., it's no use.” Only 「ところで」 standing alone at the start of a sentence changes the topic.

similar.title: さて
similar.explanation: 「さて」 is mostly used to end the opening and get to the main point. 「ところで」 usually moves to another topic or mentions something in passing.

similar.title: それはそうと
similar.explanation: Similar, both meaning “anyway, changing the subject.” 「それはそうと」 is more casual, with a nuance of “setting that aside.”

title: 〜それとも (or, in questions)
meaning: Used in either-or questions to link two options: “or.”
connection: A か。それとも B か／A か、それとも B か

senses.label: Either-or question
senses.meaning: Offers the listener two options to choose from: “or.” Usually both options end in 「か」. Only used in questions.
senses.connection: Aですか、それともBですか
examples: Would you like coffee? Or would you prefer tea?
Shall we go by train? Or by bus?

senses.label: Wondering to yourself
senses.meaning: The speaker hesitates or guesses between two possibilities: “or could it be that ...”. Often used with 「〜だろうか」 or 「〜のか」.
senses.connection: Aのだろうか。それともBのだろうか
examples: Did he forget? Or did he deliberately not come?
I can't decide whether to keep going or quit.

notes: 「それとも」 is only used in questions or when wondering, never in statements. To say “A or B” in a statement, use 「または」 or 「あるいは」.
The second option can be left out: 「〜ですか、それとも？」.

daily.title: Ordering at a restaurant
daily.description: A friend asks what you want to eat.
daily.example: Ramen? Or curry?

daily.title: Planning a date
daily.description: Deciding where to go on the weekend.
daily.example: Want to see a movie? Or go shopping?

daily.title: A clerk asking
daily.description: A clerk asks how you'll pay.
daily.example: Will you be paying in cash or by card?

work.title: Confirming the meeting format
work.description: Checking how the other side wants to meet.
work.example: Shall we hold the meeting in person, or online?

work.title: Asking the boss to decide
work.description: Asking your boss to choose between two plans.
work.example: Shall we go ahead with Plan A? Or reconsider Plan B?

etymology: Made of the demonstrative 「それ」 + the particles 「と」 and 「も」 for listing and emphasis. It is generally thought to have meant “that too (should be considered),” and later came to be used only in either-or questions.

similar.title: 〜か (or)
similar.explanation: 「AかB」 links nouns directly. 「それとも」 links two questions and stresses “please pick one.”

similar.title: または／あるいは
similar.explanation: 「または」 and 「あるいは」 are used in statements to mean “or” (「電話またはメールで連絡してください」). 「それとも」 is only for questions.

title: 〜その上 (sentence-initial: moreover)
meaning: Adds another item of the same kind to what was already mentioned: “moreover,” “on top of that.”

senses.label: Adding more
senses.meaning: Adds a point in the same direction as a good thing or feature already mentioned: “what's more,” “on top of that.” Slightly more formal than 「それに」.
senses.connection: A。その上、B (A and B are both positive or of the same kind)
examples: This restaurant is cheap. On top of that, the food is good.
She's smart. What's more, she's good at sports too.

senses.label: To make matters worse
senses.meaning: Adds another bad thing to a bad situation: “on top of that,” “to make matters worse.” Often used with 「〜まで」 or 「〜も」.
senses.connection: A (bad thing)。その上、Bまで／Bも (bad thing)
examples: I got lost. To make matters worse, it started raining.
I lost my wallet, and on top of that my phone broke.

notes: Both items must point in the same direction (both good or both bad). It cannot express contrast.
「その上で」 means “on that basis (then ...)” and is a different use.
In 「その上に本を置く」, 「上」 means “on top of” physically and is not this grammar point.

daily.title: Recommending an apartment to a friend
daily.description: Describing the good points of your new place.
daily.example: It's close to the station, and on top of that the rent is cheap.

daily.title: Complaining about a bad day
daily.description: Telling your family what happened today.
daily.example: The train was late, and on top of that I forgot my umbrella.

work.title: Recommending a candidate
work.description: Recommending a candidate to your boss.
work.example: He has a lot of experience. Moreover, he is fluent in English.

work.title: Product introduction
work.description: Explaining a product's strengths to a client.
work.example: This product is lightweight, and moreover reasonably priced.

etymology: Made of the demonstrative 「その」 + the noun 「上（うえ）」, literally “on top of that.” The physical “on top” extended to “in addition to that,” and it became a conjunction for adding points.

similar.title: それに
similar.explanation: Similar meaning. 「それに」 is more casual; 「その上」 is slightly more formal.

similar.title: しかも
similar.explanation: 「しかも」 stresses that the second point is surprising or goes further (“and on top of that, even ...”). 「その上」 simply adds a point of the same kind.

similar.title: さらに
similar.explanation: 「さらに」 is more formal and means going further in degree or adding more. 「その上」 focuses on adding one more item to what is already there.
